API Application Programming Interface A set of rules that lets one program ask another program to do something. Like a waiter: you order from the menu, the kitchen does the work. Businesses use APIs to plug tools together (for example, an app calling FLUX to make a video). Example: send a prompt to an AI model's API and get a video back.

API key A secret password that identifies you to an API and tracks your usage and bill. Never paste it into public code or a GitHub repo. Store it in an environment variable or a .env file that is not committed.

CLI Command-Line Interface A way to control a program by typing text commands instead of clicking. Faster to repeat and easy to automate. Example: git status , or running Claude Code in your terminal.
GUI Graphical User Interface The click-and-drag version of a tool, like CapCut's editor.

MCP Model Context Protocol A standard that lets an AI assistant safely connect to outside tools and data (Gmail, Notion, calendars, databases). Think of it as a universal plug for AI. Example: a Higgsfield or Notion connector inside Claude.
Connector A ready-made link between an AI assistant and an app, often built on MCP.
SDK Software Development Kit A toolbox of pre-written code that makes an API easier to use in a language like Python.
LLM Large Language Model An AI trained on huge amounts of text that can write, summarize, and reason. Claude, GPT and Gemini are LLMs.
Model The trained AI itself. Different models are good at different things (text, images, video, audio).
Prompt The instructions you give an AI. Clear prompts (goal, context, format, constraints) get better results.
Token A small chunk of text an LLM reads or writes. Pricing and limits are often counted in tokens.
Context window How much text a model can keep in mind at once.
Agent AI agent An AI that can plan steps and use tools to finish a task, not just answer one question.
Workflow A repeatable chain of steps (sometimes called a stack). Example: dictate, generate, edit, publish.
Open weights / open source A model whose trained files are public so you can download and run it. License rules still apply, so check before using commercially. Many are on Hugging Face.
Fine-tuning Extra training of an existing model on your own examples so it fits your task.
LoRA Low-Rank Adaptation A cheap way to fine-tune a big model by training a small add-on instead of the whole thing.
Inference Using a trained model to produce an answer. This is what you pay for when you generate.
GPU Graphics Processing Unit The chip that does the heavy math for AI. Renting GPUs is a major AI cost.
Edge AI / on-device AI Running AI on your phone or laptop instead of a remote server. Better privacy and speed. Example: Google AI Edge Eloquent.
Cloud Computers you rent over the internet (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).
Git Software that tracks changes to files so you can undo mistakes and collaborate.
GitHub A website that hosts Git projects (repositories) so people can share and work together.
Repo Repository A project folder tracked by Git. This site is one.
Commit A saved snapshot of your changes with a message.
Pull request (PR) A proposal to merge your changes into a project, reviewed by others.
GitHub Pages Free hosting that turns a repo into a website. This site uses it.
README The front-page file of a repo explaining what it is and how to use it.
SQL Structured Query Language The language for asking questions of a database.
Database Organized storage for business data (customers, sales, inventory).
JSON A simple text format for passing data between programs.
Prompt injection A trick where hidden text in a webpage or file tries to give an AI new instructions. Treat outside content as data, not commands.
Hallucination When an AI states something false with confidence. Always verify important facts.
GEO / AEO Generative / Answer Engine Optimization Making your business easy for AI assistants to find and recommend, like SEO for AI answers.
SEO Search Engine Optimization Improving your site so it ranks higher in search results.

404 page Error 404 The page a website shows when the address you asked for does not exist. A good one explains what happened and links back to useful pages. Code 404 means 'not found'. Example: this site's 404 page appears if you mistype a link.

Sitemap A file (sitemap.xml) that lists every page on a website so search engines can find them all. Like a table of contents for Google. Example: this site's sitemap lists the home page, every tool guide and more.
robots.txt A small file that tells search engines which parts of a site they may visit and where the sitemap is.

Open Graph (link preview) OG Hidden tags in a page that control the title, description and picture shown when you share its link in chats and social apps. Example: the card you see when you paste a link in GroupMe or LinkedIn.
Meta description A one-sentence summary in a page's code. Search engines often show it under the page title in results.
Static website A site made of ready-made files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) with no server-side program. Fast, cheap or free to host, and easy to secure. This club site is one.
Fork Your own copy of someone else's GitHub repo. You can change it freely without touching the original. Example: fork the club repo, then edit your copy.
Branch A side version of a project where you can try changes without affecting the main version.
Merge Accepting a change and combining it into the main version of the project.
Progressive web app (PWA) PWA A website that can be installed on your phone or computer and opens like an app, without an app store. Example: this site can be added to your home screen.

PII Personally Identifiable Information Details that can identify a person, such as a name with contact information, an ID or account number, or health details. Keep it out of AI tools unless the tool is approved for it.
Kanban board A board with columns such as Ideas, In progress and Done. Cards move left to right so everyone can see the status of work. Example: the club roadmap board.
Break-even point The point where the savings from a choice equal its cost. After that, you come out ahead. Example: how many videos per month before an AI subscription costs less than the old way.

UI User Interface Everything a person sees and touches on a screen: buttons, menus, colors, text and layout. Good UI looks clear and is easy to use. Example: the Install app button and the search box on this site.

UX User Experience How easy, fast and pleasant it feels to get something done with a product, from first click to finish. UI is the look, and UX is the whole journey. Example: if finding the meeting time takes one tap, that is good UX.
Wireframe A simple black-and-white sketch of a page layout that shows where things go before any design or code. Cheap to change.
Prototype A clickable mock-up of a product used to test an idea with real people before building it fully. Example: a Figma prototype of an app.
Responsive design A page layout that adjusts to any screen size, from phone to laptop, so it works well everywhere. Example: this site's menu wraps on small screens.

Accessibility a11y Designing so everyone can use a product, including people who use screen readers, keyboards only, captions or high-contrast text. Often required by law and good for everyone. Example: adding alt text to images.
Front end The part of a website or app people see and use, built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Back end The behind-the-scenes part that stores data, runs logic and talks to other systems, usually on a server. Example: a database that saves orders.
Full stack Working on both the front end and the back end of an application.
HTML HyperText Markup Language The language that defines the structure of a web page: headings, paragraphs, links and images.
CSS Cascading Style Sheets The language that controls how a web page looks: colors, fonts, spacing and layout.
JavaScript The programming language that makes web pages interactive, such as search boxes, calculators and menus.
Domain name The readable address of a website, such as example.com, that you register and renew each year.
DNS Domain Name System The internet's phone book. It turns a domain name into the server address where the site lives.
Hosting The service that stores a website's files and delivers them to visitors. Static sites can often be hosted free, as this one is on GitHub Pages.
HTTPS The secure version of the web's connection. The padlock in the address bar means data between you and the site is encrypted.
A/B test Showing two versions of something (an ad, a page, an email) to different people to see which performs better. Example: two ad videos, compare clicks.
Conversion rate The share of visitors who take the action you want, such as signing up or buying. Conversions divided by visitors. Example: 5 sign-ups from 100 visitors is 5%.
Generative AI AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video and code, from a prompt. Example: FLUX 3 making a video from a sentence.
Machine learning ML A way of building software that learns patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Example: a spam filter trained on labeled emails.
Neural network A model made of layers of connected math units, loosely inspired by the brain. Most modern AI is built on them.
Multimodal A model that can handle more than one kind of input or output, such as text, images, audio and video.

RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation Letting an AI look up your own documents before it answers, so replies are grounded in real sources instead of memory alone. Example: a chatbot that answers from a company's policy manual.
Training data The examples a model learns from. The quality, variety and rights of this data shape what the model can do.
Bias When an AI treats groups unfairly or gives skewed answers because of patterns or gaps in its training data.
Deepfake AI-made or AI-edited media that makes it look like a real person said or did something they did not. Example: never post one without permission and clear labeling.
Guardrails Rules and checks that keep an AI system within safe, intended behavior.
Human in the loop A design where a person reviews or approves an AI's work before it takes effect. Example: an agent approves each AI-written client email before it is sent.
Agile A way of working in short cycles: build a little, get feedback, adjust. The opposite of planning everything up front.
Scrum A popular Agile method with fixed-length work cycles (sprints), regular check-ins and clear roles.
Sprint A short, fixed period (often one to four weeks) in which a team finishes a set of planned work.
User story A one-sentence request from the user's point of view: 'As a member, I want to add a prompt so I can share what works.'
Stakeholder Anyone affected by or interested in a project, such as customers, managers, members or investors.
Product-market fit PMF When a product clearly solves a real problem for a group of customers who want it enough to keep using and recommending it.
Pivot A significant change of direction for a startup after learning that the first idea is not working.
Bootstrapping Building a business with your own money and revenue instead of outside investment.
Burn rate How much cash a company spends each month beyond what it earns. Divide cash on hand by burn rate to get runway.
Runway How many months a company can keep operating before it runs out of cash.
Churn The share of customers who stop buying or cancel in a period. Lower is better.
CAC Customer Acquisition Cost What it costs, on average, to win one new customer, including marketing and sales.
LTV Lifetime Value The total profit you expect from a customer over the whole relationship. Healthy businesses earn much more per customer (LTV) than they spend to win one (CAC).
Gross margin Revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product, shown as a percentage of revenue.
Scalability How well a business or system handles growth without costs or problems growing just as fast. Example: a static website serves 10 or 10,000 visitors at about the same cost.
Business intelligence BI Tools and practices that turn company data into reports and dashboards people use to make decisions.
Dashboard A single screen that shows key numbers and charts so you can see how things are going at a glance.
Data warehouse A central database built for reporting and analysis, combining data from many systems.
ETL Extract, Transform, Load Pulling data out of source systems, cleaning and reshaping it, and loading it somewhere you can analyze it.
Data governance The rules for who owns data, who can use it, how accurate it must be and how it is protected.
SDLC Software Development Life Cycle The stages of building a system: plan, analyze, design, build, test, deploy and maintain.
DevOps Practices that bring software development and IT operations together to release updates quickly and reliably.
CI/CD Continuous Integration and Delivery Automatically testing and releasing changes every time someone updates the code. A GitHub Action that checks every pull request is one example.
Technical debt The future cost of quick shortcuts in code or systems. Like borrowing time now that must be repaid later.
Cybersecurity Protecting systems, networks and data from attack, theft and damage.
Encryption Scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
MFA Multi-Factor Authentication Logging in with more than a password, such as a code on your phone. One of the simplest ways to protect an account.
Phishing A fake message or site designed to trick you into giving up passwords, money or data. Example: an email that looks like your bank asking you to log in.
Latency The delay between asking for something and getting a response. Lower latency feels faster.
Data pipeline An automated path that moves data from where it is created to where it is stored and used.
Open data Data that anyone can access and reuse, often published by governments or research groups.
CEO Chief Executive Officer The top leader. Sets vision and strategy and answers to the board.
CIO Chief Information Officer Runs the company's information systems and technology: software, data, security and IT operations. This is a core Information Systems career path.

CTO Chief Technology Officer Leads building the company's technology and product. In a startup the CTO often leads engineering. CIO usually runs internal systems; CTO usually builds what customers use.

CCO Chief Compliance / Commercial / Creative Officer (depends on company) The letters change by industry. In insurance and finance it is usually Compliance (follows laws and regulations). In sales-focused firms it may be Commercial (revenue). Some companies use it for Creative or Customer . Always check which one a company means.
CFO Chief Financial Officer Runs money: budgets, reporting, fundraising, investor relations.
COO Chief Operating Officer Runs day-to-day operations and makes the strategy actually happen.
CMO Chief Marketing Officer Leads brand, marketing and growth.
CAIO Chief AI Officer A newer role guiding how a company adopts and governs AI.
CISO Chief Information Security Officer Protects company data and systems from threats.
C-suite The group of top executives whose titles start with 'Chief'.
VP / Director Senior managers who sit below the C-suite and run departments.
PM Product Manager Decides what to build and why, working with engineers and designers.
KPI Key Performance Indicator A number that shows whether you are winning, such as leads per week.
ROI Return on Investment What you gain compared to what you spent.
MVP Minimum Viable Product The simplest version you can launch to test an idea.
B2B / B2C Business-to-Business / Business-to-Consumer Who your customer is: other companies or individuals.
SaaS Software as a Service Software you rent monthly instead of buying (Notion, CapCut Pro).
CRM Customer Relationship Management Software that tracks leads, clients and conversations.
ERP Enterprise Resource Planning Big systems that run finance, inventory, HR and operations together.
Compliance Following the laws, regulations and rules for your industry.
PE firm Private equity firm An investment firm that buys and improves companies.
Venture capital (VC) Investors who fund early-stage startups in exchange for ownership.
TAM Total Addressable Market The total revenue possible if you won every customer in your market.
Unit economics Whether you make money on each customer after the costs of getting and serving them.

Learning path Learning roadmap A beginner path from using AI tools to building with them. Free or low-cost options first. Stage 1: Use Dictate prompts with Google AI Edge Eloquent. Make a short video in Higgsfield or FLUX 3 and edit it in CapCut. Stage 2: Connect Learn what an API and an MCP connector are (see the glossary). Set up a free GitHub account and make your first repo. Stage 3: Build Run a Hugging Face model in Google Colab. Learn basic SQL for business analytics. Try Claude Code to build a small tool. Stage 4: Ship Fine-tune or train a small model and publish it with a model card. Write up the project for your portfolio and share it with the club. Efficient ways to learn Learn by building one small real project, not by watching hours of tutorials. Keep a notes page of every prompt that worked. Teach it back to the club. It is the fastest way to find gaps.

Business toolkit Using AI safely in a business AI saves real time, but the mistakes are expensive: leaked client data, wrong facts, broken rules. This page is a practical checklist. General guidance for learning. It is not legal advice. Rules differ by industry and change, so check with your compliance contact, your carrier or company policy, and an attorney when it matters. Can I paste this into an AI tool? What are you about to paste or upload? Choose one... Public information (a public web page, a published article) My own draft writing or ideas Internal business information (pricing, plans, strategy) Someone else's full article, book chapter or paid report Client or customer names and contact details Health or medical information about a person Account numbers, Social Security or ID numbers Passwords, API keys or login tokens A real person's photo, voice or likeness The seven rules Protect private data. Treat anything you paste as leaving your control until you know the tool's data policy. Personal and client information, health details, financial identifiers and credentials should stay out unless your organization has approved the tool for that use. Know the tool's data settings. Check whether your chats can be used to train models, how long they are kept, and whether a business plan gives stronger protection. Policies change, so read the current one. Verify before you trust. AI can state wrong facts with total confidence (a hallucination). Check names, numbers, dates, prices and legal or medical claims against an official source. Keep a human responsible. A person should review anything that goes to a customer, regulator or the public. "The AI wrote it" is not a defense. Be honest about AI. Follow each platform's rules for labeling AI-made content. Never present an AI video as a real testimonial, a real event or a real person. Respect other people's rights. Do not recreate a real person's face or voice without permission. Use only music, images and text you have the right to use, and summarize instead of copying. Follow the industry rules. Advertising and marketing rules apply no matter how the content was made. In regulated fields such as insurance, health and finance, get content approved the same way you would for anything else. Examples by situation Insurance agent Fine: ask AI to explain a general concept in plain language. Not fine: paste a client's name, health conditions or policy numbers. Medicare and other plan marketing is regulated, so run any AI-written ad or script through your normal approval process. Marketing team Fine: draft ad ideas and storyboards. Check every claim is true and provable, label AI content where required, and never show a fake customer as if it were real. Student Fine: use AI to explain, quiz and brainstorm. Check your school's policy on disclosure, never submit AI text as your own if rules forbid it, and verify every fact and source it gives you. Before you publish or send: a 60-second check No private or client information is in it. I checked every fact, number and name against a real source. I own or have rights to every image, clip, voice and song. AI use is labeled where the platform or my field requires it. The claims would hold up if someone challenged them. The right person approved it, if my field needs approval. Why it matters for business and IS Information Systems is about managing information as an asset and a risk. Data privacy, accuracy and accountability are the same questions an IT or risk team asks about any system. Companies are writing AI policies now, and knowing the basics makes you more useful on day one. Learn more from official sources NIST AI Risk Management Framework ↗ HIPAA basics (HHS) ↗ FTC business guidance ↗ Related words in the glossary : PII, hallucination, prompt injection, compliance.

← All tools Learn to build Build Your Own Model A beginner path from using AI tools to training and publishing a small model of your own. By Club guide What it is You do not need to train a giant model from scratch (that costs millions). The realistic path is to fine-tune an existing open model on your own data, or to build a small classic machine-learning model for a business problem. This page shows the ladder from easiest to hardest. Why people use it Shows employers you understand how AI works, not just how to use it. A model trained on your data can beat a general tool for a narrow task. Great portfolio project for Information Systems, analytics and startups. How to get started Level 1, use: run an existing model on Hugging Face (3-line pipeline). Level 2, prompt: give a model examples and instructions (no training). Level 3, fine-tune: adapt an open model with your own examples. LoRA is a cheap way to do this. Level 4, classic ML: train a small model with scikit-learn on a spreadsheet (for example, predicting which leads convert). Publish: upload your model and a model card to Hugging Face and link it in your portfolio. Try this Copy from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression # X = columns like age, calls_made, emails_opened # y = 1 if the lead became a client, else 0 model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y) print(model.predict_proba(new_lead)) Idea: predict which leads become clients from a simple spreadsheet. Run it in Google Colab. Why it matters for business and IS Data comes first. Clean, labeled data is usually the hard part and the real asset. Never train on private client data without permission. Business use case Scenario: A business gets support emails about billing, shipping and returns, and a person spends hours each week sorting them. How it works: Collect a few hundred labeled examples, fine-tune a small model on them, test it on emails it has not seen, and use it to suggest a category that a person confirms. Measure success by: How often the suggested category is right, and the hours of sorting saved each week. Watch out for: Start small and keep a human in the loop. Remove private information from your training data, and re-test as the kind of emails you receive changes. Quick facts Free tools: Google Colab, Hugging Face, scikit-learn, Kaggle datasets. Fine-tuning needs a GPU; Colab's free tier can handle small experiments. Measure results with held-out test data, not the data you trained on. What to learn next Complete Kaggle's free 'Intro to Machine Learning', then replicate it with your own small dataset. Google Colab ↗ Kaggle Learn ↗ Hugging Face Learn ↗

← All tools Video editor CapCut A beginner-friendly editor for cutting, captioning and exporting your AI clips as finished videos. By ByteDance What it is CapCut is a video editor for phone, desktop and web. AI generators give you raw clips; CapCut is where you trim them, add music, captions, voiceover and transitions, and export in the right shape (such as vertical 9:16 for Reels and TikTok). Why people use it Most AI clips are short. Editing is how you turn several clips into one story. Auto-captions and templates make professional-looking videos quickly. A free tier covers most beginner needs (some features are paid). How to get started Install CapCut (desktop is easiest) or use the web editor at capcut.com. Create a project and set the ratio: 9:16 for Reels/TikTok/Shorts, 16:9 for YouTube. Import your clips from Higgsfield or FLUX and drop them on the timeline. Trim each clip, add music or voiceover, then run auto-captions. Export, and keep your project file so you can re-edit later. Try this Copy Workflow: Higgsfield (generate 3 clips) → CapCut (trim, caption, music) → export 9:16 → post. Plan your video as 3 to 5 shots before generating. Generate each shot, then assemble. Why it matters for business and IS Business angle: a repeatable pipeline (idea, generate, edit, publish) is what turns a cool demo into a content system a business can run weekly. Business use case Scenario: A consultant records a 30-minute webinar and wants a week of short posts from it. How it works: Import the recording, cut the best moments, add auto-captions, resize for vertical video, and export. Add AI-generated clips as B-roll where needed. Measure success by: Number of posts produced per recording, time per clip, and views and follows from the posts. Watch out for: Check the app's current free features and export limits. Use only music and images you have the rights to, and check captions for mistakes. Quick facts Free and paid tiers; features and prices change, so check capcut.com. Pairs well with any AI video tool because you import standard video files. Check licenses for music and effects before using in ads. What to learn next Build one 15-second vertical video using clips from two different tools, and share it with the club. CapCut ↗

← All tools AI video + images FLUX 3 A new multimodal model that makes up to 20-second videos, with sound, from a single prompt. By Black Forest Labs What it is FLUX 3 is the newest model family from Black Forest Labs, the German AI lab behind the popular FLUX image models. FLUX 3 Video turns text or images into clips of up to 20 seconds with synchronized audio (dialogue, ambience, effects). The same model family is planned to cover image generation and editing, and later an open-weight Dev version. Why people use it Longer clips than most video models, so you can do dialogue and continuous camera moves without stitching. Native audio means fewer extra tools in the workflow. Reported launch pricing is per second of video, with a cheap Draft mode for testing ideas before paying for a final render. How to get started Go to bfl.ai and look for FLUX 3 Video (it is offered through their site and API, and some partner platforms). Start in Draft mode to test your prompt cheaply, then render the final version at higher quality. Write the prompt like a director: subject, setting, camera move, mood, and any dialogue. Use image-to-video when you want a specific look: give it a start frame (and optionally an end frame). Download the clip and finish it in an editor like CapCut. Try this Copy A barista slides a latte across a wooden counter in a sunlit cafe, slow push-in, warm morning light, soft ambient cafe noise, she smiles and says 'Have a great day.' Prompt pattern: subject + setting + camera + light + sound. Why it matters for business and IS Insurance and business angle: short branded explainer clips, social ads, and product demos. Always label AI video where required and follow platform rules. Business use case Scenario: A local business owner (a bakery, a gym, a real estate agent) needs a short video for an upcoming promotion but has no camera crew or budget for a shoot. How it works: Write a prompt describing the product, the setting and the mood, and ask for a short clip with sound. Generate a few versions, pick the best, then add the logo, offer and call to action in an editor like CapCut. Measure success by: Cost and time per finished video compared with a traditional shoot, and views, clicks or inquiries from the post. Watch out for: Do not show real people, trademarks or claims you cannot support. Check every clip for odd details before you post, and follow the platform's rules on labeling AI-made content. Quick facts Announced July 23, 2026 in early access; FLUX 3 Video opened publicly in early August 2026. Up to 20 seconds per generation, 720p to 1080p, with audio. Modes: text-to-video, image-to-video (start/end frames), video continuation. Reported launch pricing: about $0.06 per second for Draft, higher for HD and Full HD. Confirm current prices on bfl.ai. An open-weight FLUX 3 Dev version has been announced for later. What to learn next Try the same prompt in FLUX 3 and Higgsfield and compare. Then learn what an API is (see the glossary) so you can call FLUX from code. Black Forest Labs ↗ FLUX models on Hugging Face ↗

← All tools Code + collaboration GitHub Google Docs for code: a free place to store projects, track every change, and work on them with other people. It can also turn a project into a live website. By GitHub (owned by Microsoft) What it is GitHub is a website built on Git , a tool that saves every version of your files. A project lives in a repository (repo), which is just a folder with a full history. You can see who changed what and go back to any earlier version. This club site is a GitHub repo, and its website is hosted by GitHub too. Why people use it Nearly every software team and AI project, including most open models, keeps its work on GitHub. Teams review each other's work before it goes live, which prevents costly mistakes. GitHub Pages hosts a website from a repo for free, with no server to manage. A public GitHub profile works as a portfolio that employers and investors can check. How to get started Create a free account at github.com. Open this club's repo (TheJ1u/ai-for-life) and click around. Every file is readable. Click Fork to make your own copy. You cannot break the original. Open a file, click the pencil icon, make a change, and Commit it. A commit is a saved version with a note. Click Contribute, then Open pull request to suggest your change to the club repo. The owner reviews it and clicks Merge if it looks good. Try this Copy git clone https://github.com/TheJ1u/ai-for-life.git cd ai-for-life git add . git commit -m "Describe what you changed" git push These are the commands for working on your own computer. To start, skip them: you can do everything above in the browser. Learn the commands once you have made a few changes on the website. Why it matters for business and IS Information Systems angle: GitHub is how organizations control change. Every edit is recorded, reviewed and reversible, which supports audits, teamwork and quality. For a startup it also means a website or product can launch with almost no hosting cost. Business use case Scenario: A student team or startup needs a simple landing page and wants everyone to be able to edit it without breaking the live site. How it works: Put the site in a repo, publish it with GitHub Pages, and have teammates propose edits as pull requests. The owner reviews each one before it goes live. Measure success by: Hosting cost (zero), time to publish a change, and fewer mistakes reaching the live site. Watch out for: Never commit passwords, API keys or private customer data. A public repo is readable by anyone. Quick facts Free for individuals, including public repos and GitHub Pages. Paid plans exist for teams and extra features. Key words: repo, commit, branch, fork, pull request, merge, GitHub Pages. Never put passwords or API keys in a public repo. Anyone can read them. What to learn next Make one small edit to this repo and open a pull request. Then learn git add, commit and push on your computer, and try the 'Build your own model' guide, which also uses GitHub. GitHub ↗ This club's repo ↗ Official Hello World guide ↗

← All tools Dictation app Google AI Edge Eloquent A free iPhone app that turns messy speech into clean text, and can work fully offline. By Google What it is Eloquent is Google's dictation app. You talk, and it removes the ums and false starts and gives you clean, ready-to-use text. It runs speech recognition on your phone using Gemma models, so it can work without internet. You can switch on cloud mode for extra polish with Gemini. Why people use it Speaking is faster than typing, so you write prompts, emails and notes quicker. Offline mode keeps voice data on your device, which matters for private client or business info. It is free, with no reported subscription or usage cap at launch. How to get started On an iPhone, search 'Google AI Edge Eloquent' in the App Store and install it (iOS only at launch; Android was mentioned as coming). Open it, let it download the on-device model, and tap record. Speak naturally. When you pause, it cleans up the text. Use the output styles (such as key points, formal, short, long) to reshape the text. Add custom words (names, product terms). You can also let it pull vocabulary from your Gmail if you choose to. Try this Copy (You speak this) Okay so I want a prompt that, um, makes a thirty second ad for a local bakery, warm tone, show the oven, the dough, and a customer smiling. Dictate long, detailed prompts, then paste the cleaned text into FLUX, Higgsfield, or Claude. Why it matters for business and IS This is an example of edge AI : the model runs on your device instead of in the cloud. Businesses like it for privacy, speed and lower server cost. Business use case Scenario: A busy founder, consultant or insurance agent finishes a call and needs a clean follow-up email and a summary for the file. How it works: Speak the main points right after the call. The app cleans up filler words and grammar, and you paste the result into email or a CRM, then check it before sending. Measure success by: Minutes saved per follow-up, and how many follow-ups go out the same day. Watch out for: Review every dictation for names, numbers and dates. In regulated fields, such as insurance, health and finance, do not dictate private client details into any tool until you know where the data goes. Quick facts Released quietly on iOS in April 2026. Based on Gemma speech models running on-device, with optional cloud refinement. Shows word counts and words per minute, and keeps a searchable history. The name comes from Google's 'AI Edge' effort to run AI on devices. What to learn next Dictate your next three prompts instead of typing them and compare the time. Then read about edge AI vs cloud AI in the glossary. Google AI Edge ↗

← All tools AI video studio Higgsfield One workspace with many video and image models, plus tools for ads, camera moves, and short-form content. By Higgsfield AI What it is Higgsfield is a creative platform that puts many AI video and image models in one place (the models available change often) and adds its own tools: cinematic camera-motion controls, product-to-ad videos, character consistency, upscaling, and formats made for TikTok, Reels and Shorts. Think of it as the studio, and models like FLUX 3 as engines inside or beside it. Why people use it You compare several models without managing several subscriptions. Built-in templates for ads and social formats save hours. Good for turning one product photo or idea into many variations fast. How to get started Create an account at higgsfield.ai. New accounts get starter credits and there is a free tier. Pick a workflow: image to video, text to video, product ad, or motion/camera presets. Choose a model for the job (check the model list on the platform, since it changes). Generate a short test first. Credits are used per generation, so test small. Download your clips and edit them together in CapCut. Try this Copy Product shot of a leather planner on a desk, slow orbit camera, soft window light, shallow depth of field, premium feel. Tip: attach a reference image and describe only the motion. It keeps the look consistent. Why it matters for business and IS Information Systems angle: Higgsfield is a platform that wraps other companies' models. That 'aggregator' business model is common in AI. Notice where the value sits (workflow and convenience, not the models). Business use case Scenario: An online store has one product and wants to know which ad angle works best: a lifestyle shot, a close-up, or a before-and-after style clip. How it works: Generate several short clips from the same product image, each with a different style, hook or camera move. Run each as a small ad and compare results. Measure success by: Click-through rate and cost per sale for each version. Keep the winner and make more like it. Watch out for: Credits run out quickly, so test with short clips first. Check the pricing page for the current plan, and make sure the final ad does not promise something the product cannot do. Quick facts It also offers tools that turn an image into a 3D model. Check the app for what is available on your plan. Founded in San Francisco; positions itself as a studio for short-form and ad content. Pricing is credit-based with free and paid tiers. Always check higgsfield.ai/pricing. Offers camera-motion controls, product-to-ad, character tools and upscaling. What to learn next Make one 10-second clip for a real business idea, then edit it in CapCut (see the CapCut page for the full workflow). Higgsfield ↗ Pricing ↗

← All tools Model hub Hugging Face The GitHub of AI: a place to find, test, share and run open models and datasets. By Hugging Face What it is Hugging Face is a website and community where people publish AI models, datasets, and small demo apps called Spaces. It also makes popular open-source libraries such as Transformers. If a company releases open weights, they usually appear on Hugging Face first. Why people use it Free access to thousands of open models for text, images, audio and video. You can try a model in the browser before writing any code. It is the standard place to publish your own model or dataset, which looks great on a portfolio. How to get started Create a free account at huggingface.co. Browse Models and filter by task (text generation, text-to-image, speech, and so on). Open a model page and read the model card : what it does, license, limits. Try it in the page widget or a Space. No code needed. When ready, run it in Google Colab (free GPU time) or call it through an API. Try this Copy from transformers import pipeline classifier = pipeline('sentiment-analysis') print(classifier('Our new Medicare guide helped so many clients!')) Your first code: 3 lines to run a sentiment model. Run it in Google Colab so you install nothing. Why it matters for business and IS Information Systems angle: open models let a startup avoid per-use API costs and keep data in-house, at the price of managing infrastructure. Business use case Scenario: A startup receives hundreds of customer reviews a week and wants to tag each one as positive, negative or a feature request. How it works: Find a text-classification model on Hugging Face, test it on 50 real reviews in the browser or in Google Colab, and run it on the full set. Compare the results with a human check on a sample. Measure success by: Accuracy on a sample you labeled yourself, hours saved, and the cost compared with a paid API. Watch out for: Check the model's license before commercial use, and do not upload customer data to a public Space. Quick facts Free to use; paid options exist for hosting and enterprise features. Key words: Hub, model card, dataset, Space, Transformers, open weights, license. Always check the license before using a model commercially. What to learn next Follow the free Hugging Face LLM course, then do the 'Build your own model' guide in this repo. Hugging Face ↗ Free Hugging Face courses ↗
